nodes.title: Hypertensive Disorders of Pregnancy
nodes.summary: This section provides comprehensive guidance on hypertensive disorders in pregnancy, covering classification, diagnosis, and management including antihypertensive agents and seizure prophylaxis. It also details timing of delivery decisions and necessary postnatal care for these conditions.

children.title: Hypertensive Disorders of Pregnancy — Overview

children.title: Classification
children.summary: The passage classifies hypertensive disorders of pregnancy, defining chronic hypertension, gestational hypertension, and pre-eclampsia based on timing and associated symptoms like proteinuria or organ dysfunction. It also specifies criteria for severe hypertension in pregnancy using blood pressure values (systolic $\ge 160$ mmHg or diastolic $\ge 110$ mmHg).
children.content:
Chronic hypertension is hypertension present before 20 weeks of gestation or
before conception. Gestational hypertension arises after 20 weeks without
proteinuria or organ dysfunction. Pre-eclampsia is new hypertension after 20
weeks with proteinuria or maternal organ dysfunction.

Severe hypertension in pregnancy is a systolic pressure of 160 mmHg or above, or
a diastolic pressure of 110 mmHg or above, confirmed on repeat measurement
within 15 minutes.

children.title: Diagnosis and Assessment
children.summary: This section covers diagnosing hypertensive disorders by detailing proper blood pressure measurement techniques and outlining comprehensive investigations for suspected pre-eclampsia, including specific blood tests, fetal ultrasounds, and Doppler assessments.

children.title: Blood Pressure Measurement
children.summary: This passage details proper blood pressure measurement technique for pregnant women, specifying seating position, arm support at heart level, and cuff sizing. It also notes that Korotkoff phase 5 defines diastolic pressure and advises validating automated readings in pre-eclampsia against manual measurements.
children.content:
Measure with the woman seated and the arm supported at heart level, using a cuff
sized to the mid-arm circumference. Korotkoff phase 5 defines the diastolic
pressure. Automated devices under-read in pre-eclampsia and should be validated
against a manual reading at least once per admission.

children.title: Investigating Suspected Pre-eclampsia
children.summary: The passage details investigations for suspected pre-eclampsia, including blood tests (FBC, creatinine, liver transaminases, urine protein:creatinine ratio $\ge 30$ mg/mmol) and placental growth factor testing. Fetal assessment involves ultrasound biometry, amniotic fluid volume, and umbilical artery Doppler.
children.content:
Send full blood count, creatinine, liver transaminases, and a urine
protein:creatinine ratio. A ratio of 30 mg/mmol or above is significant. Placental
growth factor testing between 20 and 35 weeks helps rule out pre-eclampsia where
the diagnosis is uncertain.

Fetal assessment comprises ultrasound biometry, amniotic fluid volume and
umbilical artery Doppler at diagnosis, repeated every 2 weeks while expectant
management continues.

children.title: Antihypertensive Treatment
children.summary: This section covers management of hypertensive disorders in pregnancy, detailing agent selection (e.g., Labetalol, Nifedipine), specific blood pressure targets, and acute treatment protocols for severe hypertension, including monitoring requirements.

children.title: Agent Selection
children.summary: The passage outlines agent selection for hypertensive disorders of pregnancy, detailing first-line (Labetalol), alternative (Nifedipine), and third-line (Methyldopa) oral agents. It also notes contraindications for ACE inhibitors, ARBs, direct renin inhibitors, and diuretics.
children.content:
Labetalol is the first-line oral agent. Nifedipine modified-release is the
alternative where labetalol is contraindicated, most often in asthma. Methyldopa
is a third-line option and should be stopped within 2 days of birth because of
its association with postnatal depression.

ACE inhibitors, angiotensin receptor blockers and direct renin inhibitors are
contraindicated throughout pregnancy: they are fetotoxic, causing oligohydramnios,
renal failure and skull hypoplasia. Women of childbearing age taking these agents
must be switched before conception wherever pregnancy is planned.

Diuretics are avoided because plasma volume is already reduced in pre-eclampsia.

children.title: Treatment Targets
children.summary: The passage specifies a blood pressure treatment target of 135/85 mmHg or below for hypertensive disorders of pregnancy and warns against abrupt pressure lowering due to risks of fetal distress.
children.content:
Treat to a target of 135/85 mmHg or below. Do not lower the pressure abruptly:
placental perfusion depends on maternal pressure, and a rapid fall precipitates
fetal distress.

children.title: Acute Severe Hypertension
children.summary: The passage details immediate treatment options for acute severe hypertension in pregnancy, listing oral nifedipine, intravenous labetalol, or intravenous hydralazine. It also mandates continuous fetal monitoring during and for 30 minutes after IV treatment.
children.content:
Severe hypertension requires treatment within 30 minutes. Options are oral
nifedipine, intravenous labetalol, or intravenous hydralazine. Continuous fetal
monitoring is required during and for 30 minutes after intravenous treatment.

children.title: Seizure Prophylaxis and Treatment
children.summary: The passage details magnesium sulphate administration for eclamptic seizures and severe pre-eclampsia prophylaxis, including loading doses (4g IV over 5-15 mins) and maintenance infusion rates. It also outlines monitoring parameters, signs of toxicity, the antidote (calcium gluconate), and adjustments for renal impairment.
children.content:
Magnesium sulphate is given for eclamptic seizures and for prophylaxis in severe
pre-eclampsia. The loading dose is 4 g intravenously over 5–15 minutes, followed
by an infusion of 1 g per hour for 24 hours.

Monitor deep tendon reflexes, respiratory rate and urine output hourly. Loss of
reflexes is the earliest sign of toxicity. Calcium gluconate 1 g intravenously is
the antidote and must be immediately available at the bedside.

Reduce the infusion rate in renal impairment: magnesium is renally cleared, and
oliguria causes accumulation to toxic concentrations within hours.

children.title: Timing of Birth
children.summary: The passage outlines management timing for hypertensive disorders of pregnancy, specifying indications for birth before 34 weeks (e.g., eclampsia), expectant management between 34 and 37 weeks, and offering birth at or after 37 weeks. It also mentions antenatal corticosteroids and magnesium for neuroprotection.
children.content:
Birth before 34 weeks is reserved for uncontrollable hypertension, eclampsia,
pulmonary oedema, placental abruption or non-reassuring fetal status. Give
antenatal corticosteroids and magnesium for neuroprotection where preterm birth
is anticipated.

Between 34 and 37 weeks, continue expectant management with close surveillance
unless maternal or fetal indications supervene. At 37 weeks or beyond, offer
birth within 24–48 hours of diagnosis.

children.title: Postnatal Care
children.summary: The passage discusses postnatal care for hypertensive disorders of pregnancy, noting blood pressure peaks post-birth and requiring a 7-day review. It advises on Enalapril's use while breastfeeding and recommends annual reviews for women with pre-eclampsia due to increased cardiovascular risk.
children.content:
Blood pressure typically peaks 3–6 days after birth, often after discharge. Every
woman treated for hypertension in pregnancy needs a documented blood pressure
review within 7 days.

Enalapril is compatible with breastfeeding and is a suitable postnatal switch for
women who need ongoing treatment. Avoid diuretics while breastfeeding.

Women who had pre-eclampsia carry a lifetime cardiovascular risk roughly double
that of the background population, and should be offered annual blood pressure
and metabolic review.
